title: The outline is done. Why are you still making slides at midnight?
markdown:
# The outline is done. Why are you still making slides at midnight?

At 10:47 p.m., the hard part of the pitch may already be sitting in a document: the customer problem, the proposal, the proof, and the ask. Then comes the part nobody put on the calendar. You start copying fragments into slides, deciding what deserves a headline, hunting for a layout that does not look accidental, and shrinking type when the last slide refuses to fit.

An outline and a presentable deck are different kinds of work. The outline holds the thinking. The deck has to guide another person through that thinking at a glance. When the deadline is tomorrow, that translation can swallow the hours meant for rehearsal.

You do not need a grand design system to make a useful deck. You need decisions made in the right order.

## Start with the audience's next question

An outline often follows the writer's train of thought. A deck needs to follow the audience's questions. Before choosing a template, write those questions in the margin.

For a pitch, they might be: What is broken? Who feels it? Why is this approach credible? What happens if we say yes? For a class presentation, they may be: What am I about to learn? What is the evidence? Why does this example matter? What should I remember afterward?

Those questions give each slide a job. If a slide cannot answer one, combine it with another slide or remove it. That is usually faster than trying to decorate a weak slide into relevance.

## Give every slide one sentence to carry

The useful unit is not the bullet list. It is the sentence the audience should be able to repeat after seeing the slide.

Take an outline item such as "market problem: teams lose time assembling reporting." That is research-note language. A slide needs a claim, such as "Reporting time is stealing time from the work being reported." The supporting detail can sit beneath it, but the claim tells the room where to look.

This also catches a common late-night mistake: putting several arguments on one slide because they are related. Related is not the same as legible. If one slide argues that a problem is expensive, widespread, and urgent, the audience has to sort out the hierarchy while you keep talking. Split the ideas when each needs its own proof.

## Choose evidence before visual polish

People often open a slide tool and reach for colors first because it feels like progress. It is progress in the wrong direction when the argument is still thin.

For each claim, decide what will make it believable: a number, a short quote, a before-and-after example, a simple diagram, or a small comparison. Use only what you can explain. A chart that needs a minute of apology is probably a table or a sentence instead.

Then match the visual to the evidence. A process becomes a sequence. A contrast becomes two columns. A change over time becomes a chart only when the shape of the change matters. This sounds obvious, yet it prevents the familiar deck made of identical title-and-bullet slides.

## Make the outline do more of the work

If your outline already has sections, the fastest path is to turn each section into a question, a claim, and supporting material. A simple working format looks like this:

- Audience question: What is costing us time?
- Slide claim: Manual deck production turns preparation into a second project.
- Proof: A concrete example from the outline.
- Visual: A short before-and-after sequence.
- Speaker note: The sentence that connects this slide to the next one.

That last line matters. A deck can be visually tidy and still feel jerky when the speaker has to invent transitions in the room. Write the bridge while you have the outline open. It makes rehearsal less like memorizing fragments and more like telling one story.

## Leave room for the part only you can do

The point of speeding up deck production is not to eliminate judgment. It is to spend judgment where it pays off: checking whether the claims are fair, replacing generic examples with your own evidence, and practicing the explanation that follows the slide.

That is especially true for a pitch or a class. A polished file cannot answer the question from the back of the room. You can. The deck should make that easier by giving people a clear route into the conversation.

If you have the outline but not the evening to turn it into slides, use [Capafy's Slide Maker](https://capafy.ai/agent/8828622062?ct=capafy-distribute-slide-maker) to get the first deck-shaped version moving. Then read it as your audience would. Cut what makes them work too hard, add the proof they will ask for, and save your remaining time for the room.
